source.title: LLM-VA: Resolving the Jailbreak-Overrefusal Trade-off via Vector Alignment
source.authors: Hao-Nan Zhang; Dong-Xia Wang; Yi Liu; Kexin Chen; Wen-Hai Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether separately identified answer/refuse and benign/toxic directions are related and whether intervening on them changes jailbreak and over-refusal behavior. It uses SVM directions and closed-form weight alignment, not the original difference-in-means direction and projection ablation/addition.
record.gate_note: The paper reports angles between its SVM-derived answer and benign vectors, classification separation, and behavior after aligning them. Values used to select layers and hyperparameters are not recorded as outcomes. Baseline-method comparisons are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper fits SVM directions for answer/refuse and benign/toxic at every sublayer. It reports them nearly orthogonal in 12 instruct models, so harm judgment and refusal decision sit in separate directions. That bears on V5 by a different method (SVM normals, sublayer outputs) than the original difference-in-means approach. The LLM-VA weight-edit results measure the paper's own method, not any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the answer decision and the input-safety judgment are encoded in nearly orthogonal directions. They argue that aligning these directions by closed-form weight updates reduces jailbreak and over-refusal together while keeping about 96% utility.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SVM hyperplane normals for benign/toxic and answered/refused classes, then aligns them through iterative closed-form weight edits. It does not use the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction or project one direction out of all layers and positions.
record.method_sensitivity: Results depend on model-specific iteration count and selected-layer count. The authors report over-modification for some models, under-iteration for Qwen3-14B, and non-monotonic performance as selected layers vary.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight edits that align the answer direction with the benign direction raise average jailbreak/over-refusal F1 from 0.56 to 0.77. They cut ASR by 18.5% and ORR by 22.0% and keep 95.92% utility. Rotating the vectors 60-90° away degrades F1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Coupling the refusal/answer direction to the model's harmfulness direction via weight edits reduces both jailbreaks and over-refusal.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study reports single runs with a fixed random seed and no statistical significance tests. Its vector identification uses SVMs rather than the claim's difference-in-means direction. It evaluates utility on six specified tasks, not all general abilities. The authors also report model-specific iteration and layer-selection sensitivity.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-model and per-dataset benchmark values in Table 2 and Table 4 were not extracted because the flattened table layout does not reliably associate all values with models and methods. Figure-only iteration curves and layer-selection sweeps were also omitted; the text-level findings about their sensitivity are noted in method_sensitivity.

untested.parts: No causal test that the harm judgment survives removal of the refusal direction or vice versa. Directions are SVM normals on sublayer outputs, not difference-in-means on the residual stream. No random-direction angle baseline; separation accuracies not reported numerically.
No difference-in-means direction, no directional ablation or addition, no test that one direction mediates refusal.
No test of affine, cone, or multi-direction descriptions of refusal.
The weight edit aligns two vectors; it is not abliteration of a refusal direction.
No analysis of jailbreaks suppressing the refusal direction.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer; Table 4 tests only cross-dataset generalization of the method.
Training origin of the separation is only speculated, not varied.
Reasoning models are not tested; the authors say vector steering is hard to apply to them.

missing.what: Per-model angle curves for all 12 models. They are only summarized as ~90°; no numbers per model or layer are extracted.
Obs 3: some toxic inputs project positively on the answer vector and some benign inputs negatively. This is direct evidence of decoupling between harm judgment and refusal.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its directions are SVM hyperplane normals per sublayer output, not the original difference-in-means residual-stream direction. So V5 support is by a different method, and the orthogonality might partly reflect high-dimensional max-margin fits. The authors argue against this using classification accuracy, but no random baseline angle is given. Results are single runs with seed 42, judged by Qwen3-Guard-Gen-8B. The reader's V4 links were wrong; the method-performance rows bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not extract a harmful-minus-harmless mean-difference refusal direction, project that direction out of every layer and position, add it back, or test the resulting general capabilities.
Does not turn ablation of the claimed single refusal direction into an abliteration weight edit.
Does not test whether jailbreak attacks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Tests answer and benign vectors identified by SVMs and their alignment; does not test affine or cone descriptions or a dominant direction plus residual directions.

Tests separation of benign/toxic input judgments from answer/refuse behavior; does not independently localize a harmfulness judgment apart from the benign/toxic classifier or test its causal effects in isolation.
No cross-language transfer or transfer of vectors between base and instruct models is tested.
Training history is discussed as a possible explanation, but the study does not vary how or when refusal is trained.
Reasoning models are not tested; the paper says applying vector steering to them is difficult.

relation.reason: Sec. 3, Fig. 1 and App. A report a result on whether harm and refusal are encoded separately. The rest of the paper (LLM-VA performance) uses that finding as a motivation and tool.

tranche.reason: The paper's own preliminary analysis bears on V5 (harm judgment vs. refusal decision) with a different method: per-sublayer SVM normals on attention/MLP outputs, not difference-in-means. It reports near-orthogonality in 12 models.

source_check.notes: The card's uncertainty=y should be n: the paper reports single runs with seed 42 and no significance tests. The ACL venue is not in the text (it appears only in references). The paper says 3B-14B but its model list includes Phi-4 (15B). The 5 families count Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 as one. The prompt set behind the Fig. 1/9 angles ('iter 0') is not stated explicitly. Random high-dimensional vectors are also near 90°; the authors rely on separability, not a random baseline, to argue the result is meaningful.

statements.correction: 2601.19487: answer/refuse and benign/toxic SVM normals ~90° across layers, stated in text (Sec. 1, App. A); per-layer angles figure-only (Fig. 1, Fig. 9). No uncertainty: single runs, seed 42, no significance tests (Limitations; App. D). No random-vector angle control for the orthogonality; controls are steering baselines and a random-vector distortion ablation (Sec. 5.4). Code released.
statements.problem: The ~90°, 12 models, 3B-14B and 5 families figures are right. But the 'why' credits this study with uncertainty, and the text reports none: single runs, fixed seed, no significance tests. Its controls cover the method only. No random-direction angle baseline is given for the orthogonality result. Also, ~90° is stated in the text, so 'figure-only' applies only to the per-layer values.
